title: Portfolio Theory, CAPM and Factors
intro: Harry Markowitz showed in 1952 that what matters about an investment is not its own risk but what it adds to the risk of the whole portfolio. From that idea came the efficient frontier, the Capital Asset Pricing Model, beta, factor models and the efficient market hypothesis: the core theory behind index funds and most of professional investing.

blocks.text: Diversification in numbers
For a portfolio with weight $w$ in asset A and $1 - w$ in B, the expected return is the weighted average, but the variance is not:

Unless the correlation $\rho$ is +1, the portfolio's volatility is less than the weighted average of the two volatilities. That gap is the gain from diversification: risk falls with no loss of expected return. At $\rho = -1$ a suitable mix has zero risk. With many assets the formula generalizes to $\sigma_p^2 = w^{T} \Sigma w$, where $\Sigma$ is the covariance matrix.

widget.title: Two assets: every mix from all B to all A

blocks.text: With the defaults (a stock-like A and a bond-like B, uncorrelated), the curve bulges to the left of the straight line: some mixes of the two have *less* risk than the bond alone. Slide the correlation toward +1 and the bulge disappears; toward −1 it reaches zero risk.
How many stocks are enough?
For an equal-weighted portfolio of $n$ stocks, each with volatility $\sigma$ and average pairwise correlation $\rho$:

widget.title: Portfolio risk against the number of stocks

blocks.text: The first 20 to 30 stocks remove most of the stock-specific (idiosyncratic) risk; what remains is systematic or market risk that no amount of diversification removes. But volatility is not the only risk: a portfolio of 30 stocks still has a large chance of badly trailing the market, because a small number of stocks produce most of the market's gains. Hendrik Bessembinder (2018) found that just 4% of US listed stocks accounted for all of the stock market's net wealth creation from 1926 to 2016; most individual stocks did worse than Treasury bills over their lifetimes. Owning the whole market is the only way to be sure of owning the few big winners.
The efficient frontier

With many assets, the portfolios with the highest expected return for each level of risk form the efficient frontier (Markowitz, 1952; he shared the 1990 Nobel memorial prize with Sharpe and Merton Miller). Portfolios below it are inefficient: some other mix gives more return for the same risk. Add a risk-free asset and the best risky portfolio is the one with the highest Sharpe ratio, the tangency portfolio; every investor should hold that one portfolio, mixed with cash or borrowing to set the overall risk. That line is the capital market line. This is two-fund separation: the choice of *what* risky assets to hold is separate from *how much* risk to take.

blocks.alt: A risk-return chart showing individual assets as scattered points, the curved efficient frontier enclosing them on the upper left, the risk-free rate on the vertical axis, and a straight capital market line from the risk-free rate touching the frontier at the tangency portfolio.
blocks.caption: The efficient frontier, the risk-free rate and the capital market line touching the frontier at the tangency (maximum Sharpe ratio) portfolio.

blocks.text: Mean-variance optimization in practice

Optimizers are extremely sensitive to the expected returns you feed them: small changes swing the weights wildly, and the result tends to load up on whatever assets have the most overestimated returns ('error maximization', Michaud 1989). Practical fixes include constraining weights, using Black-Litterman (start from market-implied returns, then blend in your views), risk parity (weight assets so each contributes the same risk, usually with leverage on bonds), or simply equal or market weights. DeMiguel, Garlappi and Uppal (2009) found that a naive $1/N$ portfolio was hard to beat out of sample by optimized ones.
The Capital Asset Pricing Model
If all investors hold the tangency portfolio, it must be the whole market. Then (Sharpe 1964, Lintner, Mossin, Treynor) the only risk that earns a premium is exposure to the market, measured by beta:

items: $\beta = 1$: moves with the market on average. $\beta = 1.5$: tends to move 1.5% for each 1% market move. $\beta = 0$: no market sensitivity. Utilities and staples often have betas below 1; technology and small companies above.
$E[R_m] - r_f$ is the equity risk premium (ERP), historically around 4 to 6% a year for US stocks over T-bills, with estimates for the future often lower.
Idiosyncratic risk earns nothing, because anyone can diversify it away for free.
CAPM gives the cost of equity used in the WACC on the Valuation page.

blocks.text: A stock plotting above the line offers more than CAPM says its risk deserves (positive alpha); below it, less. Empirically CAPM has a famous problem: low-beta stocks have earned more, and high-beta stocks less, than it predicts (the line is too flat: Black, Jensen and Scholes 1972; Frazzini and Pedersen's 'Betting Against Beta' 2014). It remains the standard first model because it is simple and captures the main idea: you are paid for risk you can't diversify.
Factor models

Eugene Fama and Kenneth French (1992, 1993) found that two other characteristics explained differences in US stock returns better than beta: company size (small beat large) and value (high book-to-market beat low). Their three-factor model:

items: SMB (small minus big): the return of small stocks over large. HML (high minus low): value stocks over growth.
Momentum (Jegadeesh and Titman 1993; Carhart 1997): stocks that rose over the past 3 to 12 months tend to keep rising for some months. Profitable but prone to sudden crashes (2009).
Profitability (RMW, Novy-Marx 2013) and investment (CMA): profitable firms and firms that invest conservatively earned more. Fama and French's five-factor model (2015) adds these.
Low volatility / low beta and quality are related factors.

blocks.text: Two explanations compete: factors are rewards for real risks (value companies are fragile in recessions), or they reflect investor mistakes that persist because of limits to arbitrage. Either way, factor premia have been volatile and have shrunk after publication (McLean and Pontiff, 2016, found them about 26% smaller out of sample and about 58% smaller after publication), and hundreds of claimed factors fail to replicate (Harvey, Liu and Zhu 2016 argue a new factor should need a t-statistic above 3). Factor models are most useful for analysis: a fund's 'alpha' often turns out to be ordinary exposure to value, size or momentum that you could buy cheaply.
Arbitrage pricing theory

Stephen Ross's APT (1976) says expected returns are linear in exposure to several systematic factors (inflation, industrial production, credit spreads and so on) if arbitrage is possible, without CAPM's assumptions about investor preferences. It is the theoretical backbone of multi-factor risk models used by fund managers.
The efficient market hypothesis

Eugene Fama's efficient market hypothesis (EMH) says prices reflect available information, so you can't consistently beat the market after costs and risk adjustment. It comes in three strengths: weak (past prices can't predict future returns, so technical analysis doesn't work), semi-strong (public information is already in prices, so fundamental analysis of public data doesn't work), and strong (even private information is priced in, which insider-trading profits contradict).

items: For: most active managers trail index funds; news is priced within minutes; predictable patterns tend to fade after they are published.

Against: bubbles and crashes (1987, dot-com, 2008) that seem too large for news to explain; momentum and other anomalies; Shiller (1981) showed stock prices are far more volatile than the dividends they should reflect.

The Grossman-Stiglitz paradox (1980): if markets were perfectly efficient, nobody would pay to gather information, and then markets couldn't be efficient. Markets are efficient enough that beating them is hard and costly, but not so efficient that nobody can.
Fama and Shiller shared the 2013 Nobel memorial prize (with Lars Peter Hansen) for, in effect, opposing views of the same data.

blocks.text: The practical conclusion holds under either view: for most investors, a low-cost, diversified, market-weighted portfolio is the sensible default. Beating it requires an edge you can name, and a cost lower than that edge.
Practice

blocks.title: Two-asset risk
blocks.text: Stocks: expected return 8%, volatility 18%. Bonds: 4%, 6%. Correlation 0.1. What are the expected return and volatility of a 60/40 mix?
solution: Variance $= 0.36 \times 324 + 0.16 \times 36 + 2 \times 0.6 \times 0.4 \times 0.1 \times 18 \times 6 = 116.64 + 5.76 + 5.18 = 127.58$; volatility $\approx 11.3\%$, less than the weighted average of 13.2%.

blocks.title: CAPM
blocks.text: The risk-free rate is 4%, the equity risk premium 5%, and a stock's beta 1.4. What return does CAPM require? An analyst forecasts 12%; what is the stock's alpha?
solution: $E[R] = 4 + 1.4 \times 5 = 11\%$. Alpha $= 12 - 11 = +1\%$, if the forecast is right.
